lesson_title: The Country in One Photograph: Reading Population Pyramids
hook_text: Line up the whole country by age, fly a drone overhead — the shape you see predicts the next 30 years.
clip_script: Picture a photograph of the entire country — but everyone stands in rows by AGE. Babies in the front row, five-to-nines behind them, row after row back to the great-grandparents. Men on the left of each row, women on the right. Now fly a drone overhead. That shape is the population pyramid, and it tells fortunes. Long front row, short back rows: a country full of children, growing fast — Niger. Rows all about equal: a country coasting — Sweden. And the strange one: a SHORT front row with longer rows behind it. Fewer toddlers than adults. That country has almost stopped having babies — Japan, where families average 1,3 children and the magic replacement number is 2,1. Fast forward that shape thirty years and you get many pensioners resting on few workers. Now look for the scars: a row with a bite taken out means a war or epidemic hit that generation. South Africa's photograph? Still a wide-ish front row, a big bulge of twenty-somethings, and a taper that remembers the Aids years. One picture, the whole story — past, present and the next thirty years.
visual_style: Overhead drone shot of a crowd arranged in age rows morphing into pyramid bars; three quick silhouettes for Niger, Sweden and Japan; a thirty-year fast-forward slide.
pacing: Slow build on the photograph, three rapid shape reveals, a beat on the fast-forward, South Africa to close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson to read any pyramid — and South Africa's — like a demographer.
